simple: each piece of start-up software checks the next piece before it lets it run.
analogy: each gate guard checks the badge of the next person before letting them in.
precise: a boot sequence in which a trusted component verifies (or measures) the next component before transferring control to it, so that trust in the last stage reduces to trust in the first one and in every verifier on the way.
source: S1 of F11-01 (Systems Curriculum (this project), section 2.5 "Security and hidden components" (Secure Boot, shim, measured boot, Boot Guard and Platform Secure Boot, CSME and PSP). Opened in this build (local file); a map, not a source (AH-4).); D1 of F11-01 (UEFI Forum, "UEFI Specification" (curriculum item 12): chapter "Secure Boot and Driver Signing". Title only — not opened during this build; the Source Researcher must confirm the edition and section (dossier gate G1 open).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the first piece of the chain, which nobody checks because nothing runs before it.
analogy: the guard carved into the stone of the outer gate.
precise: a component that must be trusted because its misbehaviour cannot be detected by the chain; for a boot chain this is code and key material that run first and cannot be modified in the field (for example a boot ROM and fused key hashes).
source: S1 of F11-01 (Systems Curriculum (this project), section 2.5 "Security and hidden components" (Secure Boot, shim, measured boot, Boot Guard and Platform Secure Boot, CSME and PSP). Opened in this build (local file); a map, not a source (AH-4).); D2 of F11-01 (Trusted Computing Group, "TCG PC Client Platform Firmware Profile Specification": measurement of boot components, roots of trust for measurement.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a chain in which every stage stores the exact fingerprint of the next stage.
analogy: each guard holds a portrait of exactly one next guard.
precise: this course's name for a chain in which stage n embeds the SHA-256 digest of stage n+1 and compares it before handing over; it detects every change but forces a new release of all earlier stages for any change later in the chain (lab scenario 6).
source: R1 of F11-01 (Lab run F11-01/chain.log: g++ 13.3.0 with AddressSanitizer and UBSan; exit code 0; 2026-10-10. Forensic evidence: F11-01/forensic.log, exit code 0.)

simple: everything that must work correctly for the protection to hold.
analogy: all guards on the way in, not only the last one.
precise: the set of hardware, firmware and software components whose correct behaviour the security property depends on; in a chain of trust it includes the root and every verifier before the component in question.
source: D5 of F11-01 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security" (guide registry 4.9): trust boundaries, attack surface.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

term: TOCTOU (time of check to time of use)
simple: something is changed after it was checked but before it is used.
analogy: the guard checks a badge, turns round, and a different person walks through.
precise: a race in which the object that was verified is not the object that is executed, for example when a loader verifies an image in flash and then re-reads it from flash to run it, or when a debug probe writes to memory after the check.
source: D5 of F11-01 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security" (guide registry 4.9): trust boundaries, attack surface.) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the file format of the key lists: a header saying what kind of entries follow, then the entries.
analogy: one sheet on the gatehouse wall, headed "seal-makers" or "banned passes".
precise: EFI_SIGNATURE_LIST: a signature-type GUID (for example X.509 certificate or SHA-256 hash), the list size, a header size and the size of each entry, followed by entries of a 16-byte owner GUID and the signature data; PK, KEK, db and dbx each hold one or more such lists.
source: D1 of F11-02 (UEFI Forum, "UEFI Specification" (curriculum item 12): "Secure Boot and Driver Signing" (PK, KEK, db, dbx, setup and user mode, EFI_SIGNATURE_LIST, image verification), "Variable Services" (SetVariable, EFI_VARIABLE_AUTHENTICATION_2, time-based authenticated variables, attribute bits), "Globally Defined Variables". Title only — not opened during this build; the Source Researcher must confirm the edition and section (dossier gate G1 open).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F11-02 (Lab runs F11-02/sign_db1.log (exit 0), sb_db1.log (exit 33, ran), sb_snakeoil.log (exit 124, refused).)

simple: a firmware setting that can be changed only with a signed, dated request.
analogy: a change to the wall lists, accepted only with a steward's seal and a date later than the last change.
precise: a UEFI variable written with the time-based authenticated-write attribute; the data passed to SetVariable starts with an EFI_VARIABLE_AUTHENTICATION_2 descriptor (an EFI_TIME time stamp and a WIN_CERTIFICATE_UEFI_GUID holding a PKCS#7 signature) over the variable name, vendor GUID, attributes, time stamp and new content.
source: D1 of F11-02 (UEFI Forum, "UEFI Specification" (curriculum item 12): "Secure Boot and Driver Signing" (PK, KEK, db, dbx, setup and user mode, EFI_SIGNATURE_LIST, image verification), "Variable Services" (SetVariable, EFI_VARIABLE_AUTHENTICATION_2, time-based authenticated variables, attribute bits), "Globally Defined Variables". Title only — not opened during this build; the Source Researcher must confirm the edition and section (dossier gate G1 open).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 of F11-02 (The update bytes produced by mkvars.py and accepted by the firmware in F11-02/enroll.log and rotate.log.)

simple: replacing a signing key with a new one without breaking the machines that trust the old one.
analogy: the stewards appoint a new seal-maker and, later, ban the old one.
precise: a sequence of authenticated updates (add the new certificate to db, re-sign every boot component with the new key, deploy them, then add the old certificate or the hashes it signed to dbx) whose order decides whether machines keep booting.
source: R6 of F11-02 (Lab runs F11-02/rotate.log (exit 33), forensic_boot.log (exit 124, refused), forensic_signer.log (exit 0), sb_db2.log (exit 33).)

simple: putting a key or a program on the "never run" list.
analogy: the banned list, which wins over the guest list.
precise: adding a certificate, or the hash of an image, to the forbidden signature database dbx; an image matching dbx is refused even if it also matches db (observed in this lab: db still held the old certificate).
source: D1 of F11-02 (UEFI Forum, "UEFI Specification" (curriculum item 12): "Secure Boot and Driver Signing" (PK, KEK, db, dbx, setup and user mode, EFI_SIGNATURE_LIST, image verification), "Variable Services" (SetVariable, EFI_VARIABLE_AUTHENTICATION_2, time-based authenticated variables, attribute bits), "Globally Defined Variables". Title only — not opened during this build; the Source Researcher must confirm the edition and section (dossier gate G1 open).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R6 of F11-02 (Lab runs F11-02/rotate.log (exit 33), forensic_boot.log (exit 124, refused), forensic_signer.log (exit 0), sb_db2.log (exit 33).)

simple: an old, genuinely signed update cannot be sent again.
analogy: a steward's order dated last winter is not accepted after a spring order.
precise: for time-based authenticated variables the firmware requires the new time stamp to be later than the stored one (except for appends); a validly signed but older update is refused with EFI_SECURITY_VIOLATION (observed).
source: D1 of F11-02 (UEFI Forum, "UEFI Specification" (curriculum item 12): "Secure Boot and Driver Signing" (PK, KEK, db, dbx, setup and user mode, EFI_SIGNATURE_LIST, image verification), "Variable Services" (SetVariable, EFI_VARIABLE_AUTHENTICATION_2, time-based authenticated variables, attribute bits), "Globally Defined Variables". Title only — not opened during this build; the Source Researcher must confirm the edition and section (dossier gate G1 open).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R5 of F11-02 (Lab runs F11-02/forged.log and replay.log (each exit 33: the program ran; its SetVariable call returned Security Violation).)

simple: locking a secret inside the TPM so that it comes out only if the machine booted in a known way.
analogy: a box the notary opens only while the tally reads exactly what it read when the box was closed.
precise: the TPM binds a data object to a policy over selected PCR values; unsealing succeeds only while those PCRs hold the values in the policy. In this chapter's model: a secret plus the composite digest of the selected PCRs, released when the current composite is equal (observed in measured.out).
source: D2 of F11-03 (Trusted Computing Group, "TPM 2.0 Library Specification", Part 1 (architecture: PCRs, extend, attestation, sealing) and Part 3 (commands such as PCR_Extend and Quote) (curriculum item 53, C13).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F11-03 (Lab run F11-03/measured.log: g++ 13.3.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13, sanitizers on, exit code 0; 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.)

simple: a random number used once, so that an old answer cannot be passed off as a new one.
analogy: the messenger's fresh password.
precise: a value chosen by the verifier and included in the data the TPM signs in a quote; a quote over a different nonce is rejected as possibly replayed (scenario 4 of the lab).
source: D2 of F11-03 (Trusted Computing Group, "TPM 2.0 Library Specification", Part 1 (architecture: PCRs, extend, attestation, sealing) and Part 3 (commands such as PCR_Extend and Quote) (curriculum item 53, C13).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F11-03 (Lab run F11-03/measured.log: g++ 13.3.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13, sanitizers on, exit code 0; 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.)

simple: a signing key that lives inside the TPM and signs only reports about the TPM's own registers.
analogy: the notary's seal, which never leaves the tower.
precise: a restricted signing key created in the TPM whose private part cannot be exported; the verifier trusts its public part through a certificate chain to the TPM maker's endorsement key (not exercised in this build). In the model, a P-256 ECDSA key held by the Tpm object.
source: D2 of F11-03 (Trusted Computing Group, "TPM 2.0 Library Specification", Part 1 (architecture: PCRs, extend, attestation, sealing) and Part 3 (commands such as PCR_Extend and Quote) (curriculum item 53, C13).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of digests a verifier knows to be good.
analogy: the king's list of welcome visitors.
precise: digests of approved firmware, configurations, Secure Boot variables and boot programs, or of whole PCR values from a known-good machine, against which a replayed event log is judged; they must be updated whenever something legitimate changes, such as a key rotation.
source: R1 of F11-03 (Lab run F11-03/measured.log: g++ 13.3.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13, sanitizers on, exit code 0; 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.)

simple: a small labelled box of data: what it is, how long it is, then the data.
analogy: labelled envelopes clipped to the order.
precise: a record of a type code, a length and that many bytes of value; an image trailer of TLVs can carry a hash, a key identifier, a signature and other metadata, and a reader can skip types it does not know. In this chapter's format: 2-byte type, 2-byte length, little-endian (fwimage.h lines 119–126).
source: R1 of F11-04 (Lab run F11-04/updates.log: g++ 13.3.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13, sanitizers on, exit code 0; 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.)

simple: data that travels with a signed image but is not covered by its signature.
analogy: what is written on the envelope rather than inside the sealed letter.
precise: any byte outside the signed region; anyone can change it without breaking the signature, so a boot loader must never take a security decision from it (the forensic lab).
source: R3 of F11-04 (Lab run F11-04/forensic.log: the evidence pack, exit code 0.)

simple: a number inside the signed image that says "this release fixes everything before me".
analogy: the order's number, compared with the notch on the gatepost.
precise: a value in the signed region that the device compares with a counter it stores in memory that can only increase (one-time-programmable fuses or protected storage); an image with a lower value is refused; the device raises its counter only when an image has been accepted for good.
source: R1 of F11-04 (Lab run F11-04/updates.log: g++ 13.3.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13, sanitizers on, exit code 0; 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.); S1 of F11-04 (Systems Curriculum (this project), 17.2 "Updating safely" (signed images (MCUboot), rollback protection) and milestone H4 (goal, build and acceptance quoted). Opened in this build (local file); a map, not a source (AH-4).)

simple: a short fingerprint that says which key signed an image.
analogy: the seal's maker's mark, so the captain knows which carved impression to compare with.
precise: a hash of the signer's public key carried with the image, used by the boot loader to pick the matching trusted key; it is a hint, not a proof: the signature check with that key is the proof (lab scenario 2, fourth case).
source: R1 of F11-04 (Lab run F11-04/updates.log: g++ 13.3.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13, sanitizers on, exit code 0; 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.)

simple: exchanging two firmware slots piece by piece while writing down after each piece how far you got.
analogy: moving furniture between two rooms using a hallway, with a note on the door after every item.
precise: a sector-by-sector exchange of the primary and secondary slots through a scratch sector, each write followed by an update of a progress record in flash, so that after a power cut the boot loader repeats the interrupted step and continues.
source: R1 of F11-04 (Lab run F11-04/updates.log: g++ 13.3.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13, sanitizers on, exit code 0; 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.)

simple: the small program at the processor's highest privilege that switches between the secure and the normal world.
analogy: the guard behind the hatch of the keep's only door.
precise: code running at EL3 that handles SMC exceptions, saves and restores each world's state and sets the security state of the lower exception levels when it returns; in TF-A this is BL31, the EL3 runtime. The lab's monitor is monitor.cc and el3_entry.S.
source: D1 of F11-05 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture" (exception levels, security states, SCR_EL3, exception vectors, ESR encoding, SMC) (curriculum Track D reading).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); S1 of F11-05 (Systems Curriculum (this project), 11.2 "The common Arm boot chain" (BL31, BL32 OP-TEE, stage names quoted) and 2.5. Opened in this build (local file); a map, not a source (AH-4).)

simple: the switch that decides whether the levels below EL3 run in the normal or the secure world.
analogy: which side of the keep's wall a person is sent to when the guard lets them go.
precise: bit 0 of the Secure Configuration Register at EL3; with NS = 1 the exception levels below EL3 are non-secure and their memory accesses are non-secure, so secure-only memory is not reachable. In the lab, NS = 1 gave an abort on reading secure RAM and NS = 0 let the same read succeed.
source: D1 of F11-05 (Arm, "Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture" (exception levels, security states, SCR_EL3, exception vectors, ESR encoding, SMC) (curriculum Track D reading).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F11-05 (Lab run F11-05/tz.log: clang 18.1.3, LLD 18.1.3, QEMU 8.2.2 virt with secure=on; exit code 0 (the abort handler ended the run); 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.); R2 of F11-05 (Lab run F11-05/tz_control.log: the same with -DCONTROL_SECURE_EL1; exit code 1 (the read succeeded).)

simple: a protected place on the same processor where small trusted programs run, out of reach of the main operating system.
analogy: the keep and its servants.
precise: an isolated execution environment, on Arm built on TrustZone's secure world, with its own small OS that runs trusted applications and offers services (keys, secure storage, a firmware TPM) to the normal world through a defined interface.
source: D3 of F11-05 (OP-TEE project, "OP-TEE documentation"; GlobalPlatform, TEE Client API and TEE Internal Core API specifications (curriculum item 148).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); S1 of F11-05 (Systems Curriculum (this project), 11.2 "The common Arm boot chain" (BL31, BL32 OP-TEE, stage names quoted) and 2.5. Opened in this build (local file); a map, not a source (AH-4).)

simple: an open-source trusted operating system for the secure world.
analogy: the keep's household, organised.
precise: a trusted OS running in the Arm TrustZone secure world (TF-A's BL32 stage) that implements the GlobalPlatform TEE APIs for trusted applications; it can provide a firmware TPM, secure storage and key handling.
source: S1 of F11-05 (Systems Curriculum (this project), 11.2 "The common Arm boot chain" (BL31, BL32 OP-TEE, stage names quoted) and 2.5. Opened in this build (local file); a map, not a source (AH-4).); D3 of F11-05 (OP-TEE project, "OP-TEE documentation"; GlobalPlatform, TEE Client API and TEE Internal Core API specifications (curriculum item 148).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one small program that runs inside the TEE and does one secure job.
analogy: one servant of the keep, with one duty.
precise: an application loaded and run by the trusted OS in the secure world, reached from a normal-world client through the TEE's client interface; in OP-TEE, TAs are normally signed and verified before loading (not checked in this build).
source: D3 of F11-05 (OP-TEE project, "OP-TEE documentation"; GlobalPlatform, TEE Client API and TEE Internal Core API specifications (curriculum item 148).) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a privileged helper tricked into using its own power for someone who does not have it.
analogy: the keep's servant who reads any shelf whose number is passed through the hatch.
precise: a component that performs an action with its own authority on a resource named by a less-privileged caller, without checking that the caller may access that resource; in secure-world services, typically a pointer or address from the normal world used without checking that it points into normal-world memory (the forensic lab).
source: R4 of F11-05 (Lab run F11-05/forensic_peek.log: monitor built with -DWITH_PEEK, program with -DATTACK; exit code 0.)
related: TOCTOU (time of check to time of use)

simple: each kind of processor in a machine trusts its own signing key, not one key for everything.
analogy: each tower has its own seal impression over its door.
precise: the boot loader of each processor type holds (or has fused) the hash of a key used only for that processor's firmware; a key stolen from one build pipeline can then sign code for one processor only (lab scenario 4).
source: R1 of F11-06 (Lab run F11-06/robot.log: g++ 13.3.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13, sanitizers on, exit code 0; 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.)

simple: a signed list of which firmware versions of the different processors were tested together.
analogy: the lord's list of which towers' orders belong together.
precise: a document, signed by the vendor, listing allowed combinations of the firmware versions of a machine's processors; the system controller compares the versions actually running (each reported after that processor's own verified boot) with the list, and refuses to enter an operational state for an unlisted combination (lab scenarios 3 and 6).
source: R1 of F11-06 (Lab run F11-06/robot.log: g++ 13.3.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13, sanitizers on, exit code 0; 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.)

simple: switching off a processor's debug port for good, so nobody can stop it and change its memory with a debug probe.
analogy: bricking up the tower's back door.
precise: a one-time setting, usually a fuse or a protected option, that disables or restricts the processor's JTAG or SWD debug access; without it, an attacker with a probe can halt the processor after its verified boot and run other code, so the verified boot proves nothing about what runs (lab scenario 5). Mechanisms differ per chip.
source: R1 of F11-06 (Lab run F11-06/robot.log: g++ 13.3.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13, sanitizers on, exit code 0; 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.); S2 of F11-06 (Chapters F11-04 (image format and checks, reused), F11-05 (TrustZone) and HW303 (debug probes, JTAG and SWD) of this university. Opened in this build (local files).)

simple: the factory step that gives each new machine its keys, fuses and identity.
analogy: carving the seal impressions over the doors and bricking up the back doors before the castle opens.
precise: the manufacturing process that writes trusted key hashes and initial counters, sets the debug lock and secure-boot enable, creates or injects device keys and records the device's identity, followed by an end-of-line test that checks each of these; a mistake here is usually irreversible.
source: R1 of F11-06 (Lab run F11-06/robot.log: g++ 13.3.0 with OpenSSL 3.0.13, sanitizers on, exit code 0; 2026-10-10; untested on hardware.)
